title: Homes and space in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about housing: how much space we have, who owns it, who is waiting for it, and how much it costs.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Housing is about space, not just homes.
paras: Britain and Germany both have housing shortages, but very different ideas about owning, renting and how much room a household needs. On several of these, the room's gut was well off.
Who should get the space there is, and how, is one of the hardest questions in politics.

questions.q: In England, the typical home costs how many times the typical full-time salary (2024)?
questions.explain: The median home in England cost about 7.7 times median full-time earnings in 2024 (£290,000 against £37,600), against about 3.6 times across England and Wales in 1997. In London the ratio is about 11.
questions.source: ONS, Housing affordability in England and Wales: 2024 (March 2025)

questions.q: The UK government has set a target for new homes in England during this Parliament (2024–29). How many?
questions.explain: The target is 1.5 million homes, about 300,000 a year, a rate no government has managed year after year in half a century. Most new homes in England today are built by private developers.
questions.source: UK government, Plan for Change milestones, December 2024 (Labour manifesto pledge, 2024)

questions.q: How many households in England were on a council waiting list for social housing in 2024?
questions.explain: About 1.33 million households were on council housing waiting lists in England in 2023–24, the highest since 2014. Many wait for years: only a fraction of social homes change hands each year.

questions.q: How many homes in England had been empty for more than six months in autumn 2024?
questions.explain: About 265,000 homes were long-term empty, roughly 1 in 100 of all homes (25.7 million). The figure counts homes with nobody living in them, not unused rooms in homes that are lived in.

questions.q: On average, how much living space does each person in Germany have?
questions.sub: living space per person, end of 2025
questions.explain: Germany had about 49.5 square metres of living space per person at the end of 2025, up from about 46 in 2015, as homes grew and households shrank. It is a theoretical average: all living space divided by the population, empty flats included.
questions.source: Destatis (Federal Statistical Office), housing stock at end of 2025, press release July 2026

questions.q: What share of German households consist of just one person?
questions.explain: About 17 million of Germany's almost 41 million households, just over 41%, are a single person, one of the highest shares in Europe. About one person in five in Germany lives alone.

questions.q: Which EU country has the lowest share of people living in a home they own?
questions.explain: Germany: only about 48% of people live in a home they own, against 69% across the EU and 96% in Romania. It is the only EU country where renting is more common than owning.
questions.source: Eurostat, Housing in Europe, 2024 edition (2023 data)

questions.q: In Vienna, often praised for affordable housing, roughly what share of residents live in municipal or subsidised housing?
questions.explain: About half of Vienna's residents live in council-owned or subsidised flats; the first big council-housing programme began in 1923. The city owns around 220,000 flats itself, and about 200,000 more co-operative flats were built with city subsidies.
questions.source: City of Vienna, International Newsletter 04/2025: Vienna housing; Wiener Wohnen
